cognate: *peḱu- 'livestock': Ved. paśu- (slab) ~ Lat. pecus (slab), with Umbr. pequo, Av. pasu- (support); *wiHro- 'man': Ved. vīra- (slab, AVŚ 16.8.1 only, not adjacent to paśu-), Av. vīra-, Umbr. ueiro (support). The fully cognate two-member pair is attested only in the support witnesses
drift_or_renewal: the 'man' member renewed: Ved. puruṣa- (AVŚ 11.2, 3.28, 8.7), Lat. homo (Lucr.) and pastores (Cato); the 'cattle' member specified as go/aja/avi in AVŚ 11.2.45; Ved. vīra- still in AVŚ 16.8.1 with paśu-
shared_syntax: two-member coordination [MEN + LIVESTOCK] as the object or recipient of harm or of protection (Ved. mā no goṣu puruṣeṣu mā gṛdho; Lat. uis hominum generi pecudumque cateruis; support: Umbr. ueiro pequo ... salua seritu; Av. ϑrāϑrāi pasuuā̊ vīraiiā̊; Ved. mā hiṃsīt puruṣān paśūṃś; Cato pastores pecuaque salua seruassis)
context: AVŚ 11.2 is the hymn to Bhava-Śarva/Paśupati, the archer god whose shafts are disease: s18 lists his five paśu (cows, horses, men, goats, sheep, with puruṣā among the paśavo); s45 prays him not to covet 'our cows, men, goats, sheep'; the same hymn is the pivot of B-9e8a7, whose partner Lucr. 6.1092 introduces the plague as a force striking the race of men and the herds of cattle (hominum ... pecudum). In the slab the pair is thus carried by one cognate member (paśu ~ pecus) with the man-word renewed on both sides (puruṣa, homo); AVŚ 16.8.1 has paśavo and vīrā only inside a ten-item asmākam list, not as an adjacent pair, so it shows the lexemes but not the figure. The fully cognate figure is support-only: Umbrian ueiro pequo ... salua seritu and the Avestan 'for the protection of cattle and men' (ϑrāϑrāi pasuuā̊ vīraiiā̊), with the same prayer function as Cato's Mars prayer (morbos ... prohibessis ... pastores pecuaque salua seruassis) and AVŚ 3.28 / 8.7 (mā hiṃsīt puruṣān paśūṃś; trāyantām ... puruṣaṃ paśum). The pair is a fixed merism for the whole living household under divine threat or care, which makes the AV-Lucretius congruence (disease falling on men and cattle) more than a casual list
phrase: *wiHro- peḱu 'men (and) livestock' as merism in prayers against harm/disease

cognate: *h₁ógʷʰi- 'serpent': Ved. ahi- ~ Gk ὄφις; Ved. han- < *gʷʰen- (Gk cognate πέφνε, φόνος in the support passages)
drift_or_renewal: in the slab Greek witness the killing verb is renewed and turned passive (ἀπώλετο δουρὶ δαμασθείς 'perished, subdued by the spear'); the *gʷʰen- verb survives with serpent-monsters only in other Greek loci (κατέπεφνε, πέφνεν)
shared_syntax: [SLAYER/WEAPON] + kill-verb + [SERPENT (*h₁ógʷʰi-)] as patient, in verse: Ved. índro jaghāna ... ahe (vocative of the snake addressed); Gk ὄφις ... ἀπώλετο δουρὶ δαμασθείς (serpent as passive subject, weapon in instrumental dative)
context: AVŚ 10.4 is a charm against snakes recalling the archetypal deed, 'Indra slew (jaghāna) your first begetter, O snake' (indro ... ahe); Hdt. 6.77.2 quotes a hexameter Delphic oracle foretelling that men will say 'the dread thrice-coiled serpent perished, overcome by the spear' (δεινὸς ὄφις ... ἀπώλετο δουρὶ δαμασθείς): both are verse and both recount the killing of a serpent as a famous, retold deed. The oracle's wording is traditional epic serpent-language: a Hesiodic fragment (support) has the same δεινὸς ὄφις with a δαμ- verb (κῆλα Διὸς δαμνᾶι), and other Greek loci keep *gʷʰen- with serpent-monsters (κατέπεφνε, πέφνεν). In the slab pair only the noun is cognate and the verb is renewed, so the anchoring is weak; the inherited formula itself (HERO SLAY SERPENT) is well established

note: All 156 bundles read (pivots AVŚ 9-11; partners mostly Greek/Latin prose and AV). Nearly all bundles are root co-occurrence only. Two claims: *wiHro- peḱu men-and-cattle merism (medium; fully cognate pair only in support), serpent-slaying (low; noun-only cognate in slab). Considered and rejected as generic: head-hands-feet body merism (AVŚ 11.8.26 ~ HHMerc 240), waking/sleeping, birds eating the slain, ajara/amṛta (no Greek anchor in slab).
